rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblīs says God caused him to err, unlike Adam and Eve, who attribute their mistake to themselves.
rows.anchor: Unlike Adam and Eve, who attribute their mistake to themselves (7:23), Iblīs tells God, Thou hast caused me to err

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblīs’s accusation fits verses that seem to say God misleads some people or allows them to go astray.
rows.anchor: seem to indicate that God “misleads” certain people or allows them to go astray (see, e.g., 2:26; 40:74; 74:31).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this sense, God caused Iblīs’s failure because commanding him to bow to Adam exposed his inner pride.
rows.anchor: His Command to Iblīs to bow down to Adam was the means by which Iblīs’s inner pride became outwardly manifest (see 7:16c).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblīs’s resolve to misguide God’s creatures and beautify their actions follows from despair after banishment from God’s Presence.
rows.anchor: Iblīs’s resolve to misguide God’s creatures and make things seem fair unto them is the result of his state of despair

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name Iblīs may relate to an Arabic root meaning despair, but its likelier etymology is Greek diabolos, already in Arabic before the Quran’s revelation.
rows.anchor: though its true etymology most likely stems from the Greek diabolos, which had already entered into Arabic before the revelation of the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblīs makes people’s actions seem fair in several other passages.
rows.anchor: For other instances in the Quran where Iblīs makes people’s actions seem fair to them, see 6:43; 8:48; 16:63; 27:24; 29:38.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan also misguides through whispers, indecency, derangement, causing slips and fear, false promises, inciting evil, inducing forgetfulness, and attempting to alter revelation.
rows.anchor: Other instances include his“whispering” to them (e.g., 114:4–5), as he does to Adam in 7:20 and 20:120

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblīs’s declaration that he will mislead all except God’s sincere servants is identical to 38:82–83.
rows.anchor: I shall cause them to err all together, save Thy sincere servants among them is identical to 38:82–83.

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The straight path to God means the true path of servitude and obedience, through which one can avoid Satan’s evil insinuations.
rows.anchor: The straight path to God here implies the true path of servitude and obedience to Him (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan cannot control God’s servants; 16:99–100 says his authority is only over those who take him as protector or partner.
rows.anchor: For Satan’s inability to exercise control over God’s servants, see also 16:99–100

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Lot’s people here is tied to the commentary on 11:82–83.
rows.anchor: stones of baked clay.73–74 See 11:82–83c.

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Those who discern are people of deep reflection who recognize the reality behind outward forms, or simah.

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The standing path is a traveled road where people can see the vestiges of Lot’s destroyed people.
rows.anchor: a road upon which people travel, where they can see the vestiges of the destroyed people of Lot (Aj).

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: God guides people to the straight path of salvation, while some paths lead astray.
rows.anchor: It is for God to guide people to the straight path that leads to salvation(Bḍ), because some of them—that is, some paths—lead astray

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Some commentators call guidance God’s self-imposed obligation to guide His servants.
rows.anchor: Some commentators understood this to mean that it is God’s self-imposed obligation to guide His servants (Z)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, R
rows.claim: Other commentators view God’s guidance as bounty and generosity, not an obligation.
rows.anchor: others described God’s guiding people as an act of bounty and generosity on His part, not an obligation (Bḍ, R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse can mean that only God guides people in this way, as 92:12 says.
rows.anchor: only God can guide people in this way, as in 92:12: Truly Ours it is to give guidance

rows.speaker: Ashʿarite thinkers
rows.claim: Ashʿarites read this and similar verses to mean God does not necessarily will that all people be guided aright.
rows.anchor: For Ashʿarite thinkers, this and similar verses indicate that God does not necessarily will that all people should be guided aright (R).

rows.speaker: Muʿtazilite thinkers
rows.claim: One Muʿtazilite reading says God can compel everyone to follow His guidance but prefers to let people exercise free will and choose.
rows.anchor: Muʿtazilite thinkers, however, understood this verse to mean that, although God is capable of compelling all people to follow His Guidance

rows.speaker: Muʿtazilite thinkers
rows.claim: Another Muʿtazilite reading says God could send everyone to Paradise regardless of deeds, but wishes only those who earned it through their actions to go there.
rows.anchor: or they understood it to mean that God could guide all people to Paradise (regardless of their deeds),

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Landmarks by day and stars by night or at sea, like streams, provide guidance across times and places.
rows.anchor: other landmarks, visible along the roads by day (Q, Ṭ, Z), and the stars, which are visible by night or when at sea (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alāmāt means landmarks, including mountains (Q, Ṭ), roadside springs (Z), and winds (Q), all offering directional guidance.
rows.anchor: Landmarks translatesʿalāmāt and may include mountains (Q, Ṭ), springs along the road (Z), and winds (Q), all of which can provide directional guidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pre-Islamic nomads knew winds complexly, reflected in Arabic’s rich vocabulary; the Quran refers to some winds elsewhere.
rows.anchor: Arabs had developed complex knowledge of winds, which is reflected in the rich vocabulary in Arabic for different kinds of winds

rows.speaker: Q, Z
rows.claim: Q and Z say the singular najm can refer to stars as a single category.
rows.anchor: It may be singular in the Arabic because it is referring to stars as a single category (Q, Z),

rows.speaker: Q, Z
rows.claim: Q and Z also report that najm can refer to a particular star or constellation, such as the Pleiades, Ursa Major or Minor, or the North Star.
rows.anchor: such as the Pleiades, Ursa Major or Minor, or the North Star (Q, Z).

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The Quraysh relied on stars to navigate desert journeys and therefore should have been grateful for this blessing.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh were dependent on the stars for navigation during their travels in the desert, they should have been particularly grateful for this blessing (Z)

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: For Muslims, natural guidance sources also help find the direction of prayer in unfamiliar territory.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that everything in the heavens and earth belongs to God recurs throughout the Quran, including 2:116, 6:12, and 10:68.
rows.anchor: Unto Him belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and on the earth is repeated throughout the Quran (see, e.g., 2:116; 6:12; 10:68)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn can mean judgment as well as religion, as in the Day of Judgment, yawm al-dīn.
rows.anchor: Religion belongs to Him forever may also be rendered, “Judgment belongs to Him forever,” since religion translates dīn

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatādah understand dīn here as obedience owed to God.
rows.anchor: Many early commentators, such as Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatādah, understood dīn here as a general reference to the obedience that is owed to God

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The verse can mean obedience to God is always obligatory and His reward or punishment, His Judgment, is eternal.
rows.anchor: obedience to God is always obligatory and that the reward or punishment given by God (i.e., His “Judgment”) is eternal (Z).
